label: Apology · The Last Words
title: The Last Words
paragraphs: For the sake of only a little time, men of Athens, you will have the name, and bear the blame, among those who want to abuse the city, of having killed Socrates, a wise man. For those who want to reproach you will say that I am wise, even though I am not. If you had waited a little while, this would have come to you of itself. You see my age: I am already far along in life and near to death. I say this not to all of you, but to those who voted for my death. And to those same men I say this too. Perhaps you think, men of Athens, that I have been convicted for want of the kind of words that would have persuaded you, if I had thought it right to do and say anything at all to be acquitted. Far from it. I have been convicted for want, not of words, but of brazenness and shamelessness, and of the will to say to you the things you would have most liked to hear: me wailing and lamenting, and doing and saying many other things unworthy of me, as I say — the kind of things you are used to hearing from others. But I did not think then that I ought to do anything slavish because of the danger, and I do not regret now that I defended myself as I did. I would much rather die after such a defense than live after the other kind. Neither in a court nor in war should I or anyone else contrive to escape death by any means whatever. In battles too it is often plain that a man could escape dying by throwing down his arms and turning to beg mercy of his pursuers; and in every kind of danger there are many other ways to escape death, if a man is willing to do and say anything. But I suspect, gentlemen, that the hard thing is not to escape death. It is much harder to escape wickedness, for it runs faster than death. And now I, being slow and old, have been caught by the slower runner; and my accusers, being clever and quick, by the faster, by evil. Now I go away condemned by you to death; and they go condemned by the truth to wickedness and injustice. I abide by my penalty, and they by theirs. Perhaps it had to be so, and I think it is fair enough.

And now I want to prophesy to you, you who have voted against me. For I am now at the point where people most often prophesy, when they are about to die. I tell you, you men who have killed me, that punishment will come upon you straight after my death, far harsher, by Zeus, than the death you have given me. You have done this now thinking that you would be freed from having to give an account of your lives. But I tell you it will turn out quite the opposite. There will be more men to call you to account — men I was holding back until now, though you did not see it. They will be harsher, being younger, and you will be more indignant. If you think that by killing people you will stop anyone from reproaching you for not living rightly, you are mistaken. That way of escape is neither really possible nor honorable. The finest and easiest way is not to cut other people down, but to make oneself as good as possible. With that prophecy to you who voted against me, I take my leave.

But with those who voted to acquit me I would gladly talk over this thing that has happened, while the officers are busy and I am not yet on my way to the place where I must die. Stay with me, gentlemen, for that little time. Nothing prevents our talking with one another while we may. To you, as my friends, I want to show the meaning of what has just happened to me. For to me, judges — and in calling you judges I would be calling you by your right name — a wonderful thing has happened. The prophetic power I am used to, that of the divine sign, was always very frequent in all the time before, and opposed me even in very small things, if I was about to do something that was not right. And now there has happened to me what you see for yourselves, what one might think, and what is commonly held, to be the worst of evils. Yet the god's sign did not oppose me when I left my house this morning, nor when I came up here to the court, nor at any point in my speech when I was about to say something. And yet in other talks it has often stopped me in the middle of what I was saying. But now, in this affair, it has not opposed me anywhere, in anything I did or said. What do I take to be the reason? I will tell you. It may be that what has happened to me is a good thing, and those of us who think death is an evil cannot be right. I have had a strong proof of this: the familiar sign would surely have opposed me if I had not been about to do something good.

Let us consider in this way too how much hope there is that it is a good thing. Being dead is one of two things. Either it is like being nothing, and the dead man has no perception of anything; or, as we are told, it is a change, a moving of the soul from this place to another. Now if there is no perception at all, but it is like a sleep in which the sleeper does not even dream, death would be a wonderful gain. For I think that if someone had to pick out the night in which he slept so soundly that he did not even dream, and set beside it all the other nights and days of his life, and had to consider and say how many days and nights in his life he had spent better and more pleasantly than that night — I think that not just a private person but the Great King himself would find them easy to count beside the other days and nights. If death is like that, then, I call it a gain; for in that case all of time seems no more than a single night. But if death is a kind of journey from here to another place, and what we are told is true, that all the dead are there, what greater good could there be than this, judges? If a man arrives in Hades, rid of these men here who claim to be judges, and finds the true judges, who are said to sit in judgment there, Minos and Rhadamanthus and Aeacus and Triptolemus, and the other demigods who were just in their own lives, would that be a poor journey? Or again, to keep company with Orpheus and Musaeus and Hesiod and Homer — what would any of you not give for that? I am willing to die many times over, if these things are true. For me especially it would be a wonderful way to spend my time there, whenever I met Palamedes, or Ajax the son of Telamon, or any other of the men of old who died by an unjust judgment, to compare what happened to me with what happened to them. That, I think, would not be unpleasant. And best of all, I could go on examining and questioning the people there as I do those here, to find out who among them is wise, and who thinks he is and is not. What would one not give, judges, to examine the man who led the great army against Troy, or Odysseus, or Sisyphus, or countless others one could name, men and women both? To talk with them there, and keep company with them, and examine them, would be happiness beyond measure. At any rate, the people there surely do not put a man to death for it. They are happier than the people here in other ways, and for the rest of time they are immortal, if what we are told is true.

But you too, judges, must be of good hope in the face of death, and keep this one truth in mind: that nothing evil can happen to a good man, either in life or after death, and his affairs are not neglected by the gods. What has happened to me now has not come of itself. It is clear to me that it was better for me to die now and be rid of my troubles. That is why the sign never turned me back, and why I am not at all angry with those who voted against me, or with my accusers. Yet it was not with this in mind that they voted against me and accused me; they thought they were harming me. For that they deserve blame. Still, I ask this much of them. When my sons grow up, gentlemen, punish them by troubling them in the very same way I troubled you, if they seem to you to care for money or anything else before virtue. And if they think they are something when they are nothing, reproach them as I reproached you, for not caring about the right things, and for thinking they are something when they are worth nothing. If you do this, I will have been treated justly by you, I myself and my sons.
But now it is time to go, I to die and you to live. Which of us goes to the better thing is clear to no one but the god.

divergences.phrase: ὁπότεροι δὲ ἡμῶν ἔρχονται ἐπὶ ἄμεινον πρᾶγμα, ἄδηλον παντὶ πλὴν ἢ τῷ θεῷ
divergences.older: Which is better God only knows.
divergences.lectio: Which of us goes to the better thing is clear to no one but the god.
divergences.note: Jowett's close is an English idiom and a Christian one. The Greek is plainer and stranger: 'unclear to everyone except the god', the god being the one who has stood behind the whole speech, Apollo at Delphi. The edition keeps the word order, with the god last.

divergences.older: O my judges—for you I may truly call judges
divergences.lectio: judges — and in calling you judges I would be calling you by your right name
divergences.note: Through the whole trial Socrates has said 'men of Athens' and never 'judges', the usual address to a court. He gives the title only now, and only to those who voted to acquit. The edition keeps the two forms of address strictly apart so the moment can be seen.

divergences.phrase: οὐκ ἔστιν ἀνδρὶ ἀγαθῷ κακὸν οὐδὲν οὔτε ζῶντι οὔτε τελευτήσαντι
divergences.older: no evil can happen to a good man, either in life or after death
divergences.lectio: nothing evil can happen to a good man, either in life or after death
divergences.note: Kept very close to Jowett because the Greek is that plain. It answers 30c–d, where Socrates says a better man cannot be harmed by a worse: being killed is not the harm; doing wrong is.
